questions.q: An alkane has a relative molecular mass of 72.0. What is its molecular formula? (\(A_{\text{r}}\): C 12.0, H 1.0)
questions.solution: Alkanes are \(\mathrm{C_{n}H_{2n+2}}\), so \(M_{\text{r}}\) = 12.0n + 1.0(2n + 2) = 14n + 2. Then 14n + 2 = 72.0, so n = 5 and the formula is \(\mathrm{C_{5}H_{12}}\). (\(\mathrm{C_{5}H_{10}}\) has \(M_{\text{r}}\) 70.0 and is not an alkane.)

questions.q: Cyclohexane and hex-1-ene both have the formula \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{12}}\). Which statement about cyclohexane is correct?

options.A: It is a saturated hydrocarbon, and its general formula is \(\mathrm{C_{n}H_{2n}}\).
options.B: It is an unsaturated hydrocarbon, because it has the same molecular formula as hex-1-ene.
options.C: It is a saturated hydrocarbon, and its general formula is \(\mathrm{C_{n}H_{2n+2}}\).
options.D: It decolourises bromine water quickly in the dark, like hex-1-ene.

questions.solution: Cyclohexane contains only C–C and C–H single bonds, so it is saturated. Closing the ring removes two hydrogen atoms compared with hexane, so cycloalkanes are \(\mathrm{C_{n}H_{2n}}\), the same as alkenes. (Having no C=C, it does not decolourise bromine water in the dark.)

questions.q: How does fractional distillation separate crude oil into fractions?

options.A: By boiling point, in a column that is hottest at the bottom and coolest at the top
options.B: By boiling point, in a column that is hottest at the top and coolest at the bottom
options.C: By density, with the densest fraction collected at the top of the column
options.D: By breaking the C–C bonds in long-chain molecules to make shorter ones

questions.solution: Vaporised crude oil rises up a column with a temperature gradient. Each fraction condenses where the temperature falls below its boiling point: long chains with high boiling points near the hot bottom, short chains near the cool top. (Breaking C–C bonds is cracking, a chemical change.)

questions.q: Pentane boils at 36 °C, but its isomer 2,2-dimethylpropane boils at 10 °C. Which statement best explains the difference?

figure.alt: Skeletal formulae of pentane, a straight five-carbon chain, and its isomer 2,2-dimethylpropane, a compact molecule with one carbon joined to four others.

options.A: The branched molecules have fewer electrons, so the London forces between them are weaker.
options.B: Pentane has stronger C–C bonds, which must be broken when it boils.
options.C: Pentane molecules are polar, so they have permanent dipole forces between them.
options.D: The branched molecules have less surface contact with each other, so the London forces between them are weaker.

questions.solution: Both are \(\mathrm{C_{5}H_{12}}\), so they have the same number of electrons. The near-spherical 2,2-dimethylpropane molecules touch over a smaller area, so the London forces between them are weaker and less energy is needed to separate them. (Boiling breaks no covalent bonds, and alkanes are non-polar.)

questions.q: Which describes the conditions and main products of catalytic cracking?

options.A: High pressure and high temperature, no catalyst; a high percentage of alkenes
options.B: Slight pressure, high temperature and a zeolite catalyst; a high percentage of alkenes
options.C: High pressure, low temperature and an iron catalyst; mainly motor fuels and aromatic hydrocarbons
options.D: Slight pressure, high temperature and a zeolite catalyst; mainly motor fuels and aromatic hydrocarbons

questions.solution: Catalytic cracking uses a zeolite catalyst at high temperature and only slight pressure, and gives mainly branched alkanes, cycloalkanes and aromatic hydrocarbons for motor fuels. Thermal cracking uses high temperature and high pressure without a catalyst and gives a high percentage of alkenes.

questions.q: Tetradecane, \(\mathrm{C_{14}H_{30}}\), is cracked to give octane, \(\mathrm{C_{8}H_{18}}\), and ethene only. How many molecules of ethene form from each molecule of tetradecane?
questions.solution: Carbon left after octane: 14 − 8 = 6. Each ethene, \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}}\), has 2 carbons, and 6 ÷ 2 = 3. Hydrogen check: 18 + 3 × 4 = 30. So 3 molecules: \(\mathrm{C_{14}H_{30} \rightarrow C_{8}H_{18} + 3C_{2}H_{4}}\). (Counting the six leftover carbon atoms as six molecules leads to 6.)

questions.q: Why do oil refineries crack long-chain alkanes?

options.A: Long-chain alkanes contain sulfur, and cracking removes it before the fuel is burned.
options.B: Crude oil contains more long-chain alkanes than are needed; cracking turns them into shorter alkanes and alkenes that are in greater demand and more valuable.
options.C: Cracking joins short-chain alkanes into the longer chains needed for lubricating oils.
options.D: Long-chain alkanes cannot be separated by fractional distillation, so they must be cracked first.

questions.solution: The heavy fractions are produced in excess of demand, while petrol and alkenes such as ethene (for polymers) are in short supply. Cracking breaks C–C bonds in the surplus long chains to make these more valuable products. (Removing sulfur is a separate process, and cracking makes shorter chains, not longer ones.)

questions.q: Which process is shown, and why is it used?

figure.alt: Hexane, a straight six-carbon chain, is converted with a catalyst and heat into a six-carbon chain with one branch.

options.A: Cracking: shorter-chain alkanes are in greater demand.
options.B: Reforming: branched-chain alkanes are needed to make alkenes for polymers.
options.C: Reforming: branched-chain alkanes burn more efficiently in petrol engines.
options.D: Isomerisation by cracking: the product has a higher boiling point and is easier to store.

questions.solution: The molecular formula is unchanged and the chain becomes branched: this is reforming, which turns straight-chain alkanes into branched-chain alkanes and cyclic hydrocarbons. These burn more smoothly and efficiently in engines. (No C–C bond is broken to make smaller molecules, so it is not cracking.)

questions.q: The equation for the complete combustion of hexane is \(\mathrm{2C_{6}H_{14} + \mathit{x}O_{2} \rightarrow 12CO_{2} + 14H_{2}O}\). What is the value of x?
questions.solution: Count oxygen atoms on the right: 12 × 2 + 14 × 1 = 38. Each \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\) supplies two atoms, so x = 38 ÷ 2 = 19. (Forgetting to halve the 38 atoms is the usual slip.)

questions.q: Many homes in Ghana and Nigeria cook with LPG. A cylinder holds 13.0 kg of gas; assume it is pure butane, \(\mathrm{C_{4}H_{10}}\) (\(M_{\text{r}} = 58.0\)). What mass of carbon dioxide (\(M_{\text{r}} = 44.0\)) forms when it all burns completely?
questions.solution: \(\mathrm{2C_{4}H_{10} + 13O_{2} \rightarrow 8CO_{2} + 10H_{2}O}\): 4 mol \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) per mole of butane. Amount of butane = 13 000 ÷ 58.0 = 224.1 mol, so \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) = 4 × 224.1 = 896.6 mol. Mass = 896.6 × 44.0 g = 39.4 kg. (Missing the factor of 4 leads to 9.86 kg.)

questions.q: How is nitrogen monoxide, NO, formed in a car engine?

options.A: Nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at the very high temperature in the engine.
options.B: It is formed by incomplete combustion of the hydrocarbon fuel.
options.C: Nitrogen reacts with water vapour formed by the combustion.
options.D: The catalytic converter oxidises nitrogen from the air.

questions.solution: The air drawn into the engine is mostly nitrogen. At the very high temperatures of combustion, its strong triple bond can break, and it reacts with oxygen: \(\mathrm{N_{2} + O_{2} \rightarrow 2NO}\). (Incomplete combustion gives carbon monoxide and soot; the catalytic converter removes NO.)

questions.q: Which equation shows a reaction in a catalytic converter that removes both carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide?
questions.solution: On the platinum–rhodium surface, CO is oxidised and NO is reduced: \(\mathrm{2CO + 2NO \rightarrow 2CO_{2} + N_{2}}\). Both products are naturally in air. (The \(\mathrm{N_{2}O}\) product is itself a pollutant, and the last equation makes NO rather than removing it.)

questions.q: Why is sulfur dioxide released by burning fuels a problem?

options.A: It is the main greenhouse gas released by burning fuels.
options.B: It binds to haemoglobin and stops the blood carrying oxygen.
options.C: It reacts with unburned hydrocarbons to form carbon particulates.
options.D: It is an acidic oxide that dissolves in rain to form acid rain.

questions.solution: Sulfur impurities burn to \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\), an acidic gas. It dissolves in water and is oxidised to sulfuric acid, giving acid rain that damages buildings, lakes and trees. (Carbon dioxide is the main greenhouse gas; carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin.)

questions.q: Bioethanol made from sugar cane is sometimes described as "carbon neutral". Which is the best evaluation of this claim?

options.A: It is completely carbon neutral, because burning ethanol produces no carbon dioxide.
options.B: The carbon dioxide released when it burns was absorbed by the cane as it grew, but fossil fuels used in farming, processing and transport mean it is not fully carbon neutral.
options.C: It is completely carbon neutral, because sugar cane is a renewable resource.
options.D: It is not carbon neutral, because ethanol releases far more carbon dioxide per mole than petrol does.

questions.solution: Burning ethanol does release \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) (\(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}OH + 3O_{2} \rightarrow 2CO_{2} + 3H_{2}O}\)), but the same amount was taken in by photosynthesis. Energy from fossil fuels for fertiliser, harvesting, fermentation, distillation and transport adds extra \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\), so it is close to, but not fully, carbon neutral.

questions.q: What is a radical?

options.A: A positively charged ion formed when a bond breaks
options.B: A species with a lone pair of electrons that it can donate
options.C: A species with an unpaired electron
options.D: Any atom with an incomplete outer shell of electrons

questions.solution: A radical has an unpaired electron, shown by a dot, for example \(\mathrm{Cl\bullet}\). It forms when a covalent bond breaks homolytically, each atom taking one electron. (A lone-pair donor is a nucleophile; ions form by heterolytic fission.)

questions.q: Which equation is the initiation step in the reaction of methane with chlorine in ultraviolet light?
questions.solution: Ultraviolet light provides the energy to break the weakest bond, Cl–Cl, homolytically: \(\mathrm{Cl_{2} \rightarrow 2Cl\bullet}\). The C–H bond is much stronger and is not broken by UV light. (The last equation is the first propagation step.)

questions.q: Which step in the chlorination of methane is shown?

figure.alt: Displayed formulae: a methyl radical, with a dot on its carbon, plus a chlorine molecule, react to give chloromethane plus a chlorine atom with a dot.

questions.solution: A radical reacts with a molecule to give a product and a new radical: \(\mathrm{\bullet CH_{3} + Cl_{2} \rightarrow CH_{3}Cl + Cl\bullet}\). This is the second propagation step; the chlorine radical it regenerates starts the first step again. (Termination removes radicals: two radicals join.)

questions.q: Dichloromethane also forms when methane reacts with chlorine in UV light. Which is a propagation step that leads to it?
questions.solution: A propagation step has one radical on each side. A chlorine radical removes a hydrogen atom from chloromethane: \(\mathrm{Cl\bullet + CH_{3}Cl \rightarrow \bullet CH_{2}Cl + HCl}\); then \(\mathrm{\bullet CH_{2}Cl + Cl_{2} \rightarrow CH_{2}Cl_{2} + Cl\bullet}\). (Two radicals joining is termination; the radical-free equation is the overall reaction.)

questions.q: Methane is reacted with chlorine in UV light to make chloromethane. Why is an excess of methane used?

options.A: To make sure that all the methane reacts.
options.B: Because methane is needed to absorb the UV light and start the reaction.
options.C: To make it more likely that chlorine radicals collide with methane rather than with chloromethane, reducing further substitution.
options.D: To speed up the termination steps, so the reaction stops quickly.

questions.solution: Chloromethane can itself be attacked by chlorine radicals, giving dichloromethane and more highly substituted products. With methane in excess, a chlorine radical is much more likely to hit a methane molecule, so chloromethane is the main product. (UV light is absorbed by chlorine, breaking the Cl–Cl bond.)

questions.q: The alkane shown reacts with chlorine in UV light. How many structural isomers with the formula \(\mathrm{C_{5}H_{11}Cl}\) can form?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a branched alkane: a four-carbon chain with a one-carbon branch on the second carbon.

questions.solution: The compound is 2-methylbutane. Its two methyl groups on carbon 2 are equivalent, so there are four different kinds of carbon to put the Cl on: 1-chloro-2-methylbutane, 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, 2-chloro-3-methylbutane and 1-chloro-3-methylbutane. So 4 isomers. (Counting the two equivalent methyl groups separately leads to 5.)
